perspective:
Harold Padilla’s available information:

- He is Harold Padilla, a project manager. He knows his own feelings and decisions: he feels frustrated/anxious that his project team seems unmotivated and progress is suffering.
- He knows Arthur Begum as his friend and a police officer, someone he trusts for advice.
- At the coffee shop, Harold told Arthur that his team seems unmotivated and it is affecting progress. He heard Arthur advise understanding each team member’s individual motivation and having one-on-one conversations so people feel valued and understood. Harold decided to try this and felt more hopeful.
- Harold then held a team meeting. He proposed one-on-one chats to understand what motivates each person. He heard Team Member 1 say it could be helpful, and Team Member 2 say they were open to it. Harold said he would schedule time with each person and wanted the project to succeed together.
- Later, Harold noticed the team still was not responding well. He felt disappointed and worried. He told Arthur he had tried the suggestions but the team still wasn’t responding. He heard Arthur say there may be deeper issues: personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors, and that Harold might need to dig deeper. Harold decided to set up another round of meetings.
- In those one-on-one meetings, Harold asked team members to share concerns or problems. He heard Team Member 1 say there was tension between a few team members affecting work. He heard Team Member 2 say they felt overwhelmed by the workload, stressed, and found it hard to stay motivated. Harold said he would look into resolving conflicts and redistribute tasks, and that their well-being was important.
- Harold later told the team he had heard their concerns and would implement regular feedback sessions and team-building activities. He heard Team Member 1 say that sounded great and would help, and Team Member 2 agree that it was good concerns were being addressed. Harold said they should work together and that their input and well-being were crucial.

He does not have access to hidden/private thoughts, unspoken team conflicts, Arthur’s internal reasoning, or narrator-only commentary.
